How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability).

Provenance, kept so that a TRACE Research Object (TRO) declaration of the run can be written later from a stored result (metacheck #404; the helpers are in R/provenance.R). Only when code was run (execute = TRUE): * run_results$started_at, run_results$ended_at: when each run of a script started and ended (ISO 8601, UTC, milliseconds); NA for a script that was not started. A script run again in a later pass has the times of its last run. A TRO uses them for each trov:TransparentResearchPerformance. * run_results$exit_status: the exit status of the process that ran the script (0 = ended normally); NA when the process did not report one (a time limit, or Docker failing to start the container). * artifacts: one row per file, with stage (deposit: as downloaded from the repository, hashed from the downloaded file; before_run: the run folder just before the first script ran, after metacheck’s own changes, such as rewritten paths and unpacked archives; after_run: only the files the scripts made (status new), changed (changed) or removed (removed), as an unchanged file is the one listed before the run), path (relative to the run folder, as valid UTF-8, a byte of another encoding written as <xx>), size (bytes), sha256, mime_type (by extension, NA when unknown), source (the file’s address in the repository, for deposit). The package libraries metacheck installs in the run folder are left out, as are metacheck’s own files there (a script’s runner, and the statistical output it writes in statistical_output/). Files metacheck itself copied or made between passes (see modifications, output_copied, file_placed) show in after_run too. A TRO uses the rows as trov:ResearchArtifacts and each stage as a trov:ArtifactArrangement. * modifications$sha256_before, modifications$sha256_after: the hash of the changed script as downloaded and as it ran; NA when the script is not at the same path in both (a script made from an R Markdown file). * environment: the system that ran the code (trov:TransparentResearchSystem in a TRO): metacheck_version, started_at, ended_at, host (R version, platform, operating system), sandbox, network_isolated (TRUE only when every Docker run had --network none; the process sandbox does not stop the network), internet, timeout_per_script, total_timeout, python_local (the Python run outside Docker and its version), and docker: runs (for each kind of run, r_run, r_install, python_run, python_install, the image and the docker run arguments, such as --network none, --read-only, --cap-drop ALL, no-new-privileges, the process limit and the memory and processor limits) and images (for each image, its ID and digests from docker image inspect, its creation time and the R and Python versions its environment declares).

run_results$checked says what the run of each script shows about the code, in five groups, so that a script that does not reproduce is kept apart from one the check could not test: ran (it ran to the end); code_error (it did not reproduce: it stopped with an error of the code or the deposit, could not be read, or needs a file the deposit does not hold); dependency (a package or program was not available: a package that could not be installed or was not loaded, a program outside R and Python, a system library, or R crashing in a package’s compiled code); time (it did not finish within the time limit for one script, or was not started because the time for all scripts had run out); and not_checkable (it could not be checked automatically: it needs a person, the internet, a key or another setting of the authors’ computer, one platform such as Google Colab, Windows or OpenSAFELY, more memory than the run allows, a file that was not downloaded, a screen, or a program that runs it, or it is a file of a package of the code that Python runs only as a module of that package). It is NA for files run inside another script, files that are not an analysis, files not read, and a Docker failure. summary_table counts each group (repro_ran_n, repro_code_error_n, repro_dependency_n, repro_time_n, repro_not_checkable_n), and the report’s first sentence gives them. The traffic light reflects the static readiness signals by default; a script in code_error that stopped with an error makes it red, as a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure, and a script in one of the other three groups keeps it from being green. Calls that need a screen, which the run does not have (dev.print(), dev.copy2pdf(), dev.copy2eps(), savePlot(), windows(), win.graph(), x11(), quartz(), View()), are replaced before the run by calls that need none, which modifications records as screen_call_replaced. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Felt presence (FP), the sense that another agent is nearby without corresponding sensory evidence, occurs across neurological, psychiatric and non-clinical populations. Prior work links childhood imaginary companions (ICs) to anomalous and presence-related experience; we asked whether this link carries the spatial and perspectival signature predicted by a bodily selfconsciousness (BSC) account. In 185 adults without psychiatric or neurological diagnoses (45 with and 140 without a childhood IC history), IC-positive participants retrospectively reported their companion's location, distance and perspective, and all participants completed the Sensed Presence Questionnaire (SenPQ) and a dissociation questionnaire. IC-positive adults scored significantly higher on the SenPQ. This supports the continuity prediction. There was no significant difference between the two groups in dissociation scores. Of the IC-positive participants, 88.9% (40 of 45) recalled their companion from a body-referenced perspective, that is, from a first-person or a mixed first-and third-person viewpoint. This result offers tentative support for the perspective prediction, because three of the four fixed response options were bodyreferenced and therefore favoured this answer. In 66.7% (76 of 114) of the distance estimates given for directions in which the companion had appeared, participants placed it within 70 cm of the body, the operational boundary of peripersonal space (PPS) adopted in this study. This proportion was significantly greater than one half and therefore offers moderate support for the peripersonal prediction. Companions were most often localised in front of and beside the body, a spatial distribution that differs from that of adult FP, which is typically experienced behind or beside the body. Taken together, the findings are consistent with prior work linking ICs to presence-related experience and they provide partial evidence that this link reflects the mechanisms proposed by a BSC account.

1. Introduction

>Introduction

1.1 Imaginary Companions, Felt Presence, and the Bodily Self

Childhood is a pivotal stage of human development, marked by an extraordinary capacity to generate rich inner worlds populated by unseen companions (Taylor, 1999; Taylor et al., 2020).

Among the most intriguing aspects of early childhood is the widespread phenomenon of imaginary companions (ICs) invisible, personified entities with whom children form sustained relationships, typically between the ages of three and eight (Moriguchi & Todo, 2018 , 2019; Taylor, 1999; Wigger, 2018). The phenomenon has been systematically documented since the early twentieth century (Ames & Learned, 1946; Bender & Vogel, 1941; Kirkpatrick, 1908; Svendsen, 1934), with early reports already noting marked heterogeneity in form including animal companions, opposite-sex figures, and entire imagined families and in number, with some children reporting multiple coexisting companions (Bender & Vogel, 1941; Ames & Learned, 1946). Svendsen (1934) defined the imaginary companion as "an invisible character, named and referred to in conversation with other persons or played with directly for a period of time, at least several months, having an air of reality for the child, but no apparent objective basis" (p. 988). Although Svendsen's account includes observations consistent with ICs occupying physical space, such as a companion accorded a seat at the family table, the systematic claim that ICs are treated as space-occupying entities is better supported by more recent work (Madsen & Gleason, 2025; Taylor & Aguiar, 2024), an observation that prefigures contemporary accounts in which internally generated agent representations are anchored within the spatial coordinates of the bodily self. A recent metaanalysis of cross-cultural studies estimated that approximately one-quarter to one-third of children report IC experiences at some point during development (Moriguchi & Todo, 2018) although earlier surveys using broader definitional criteria have reported substantially higher prevalence rates of up to ~65% (Singer & Singer, 1990; Taylor, 1999). Much of this variation is definitional rather than substantive. Studies applying the narrower criterion of a wholly invisible companion report lower rates than those admitting personified objects, in which a physically present toy or object is attributed a stable personality and treated as a social partner. The higher prevalence figures reported in the literature largely reflect the inclusion of this visible, object-based category.

A question that follows from this prior work is as follows: Are childhood imaginary companions spatially anchored within the body's immediate action field, and do they rely on the same embodied self-representational mechanisms that give rise to FP experiences in adults?

To address this question, the present research draws on two bodies of literature: the developmental science of imaginary companions (see Armah & Landers-Potts, 2021, for a comprehensive review) and the cognitive neuroscience of felt presence and its link to theories of bodily self-consciousness (Barnby et al., 2023; Hara, Blanke, & Kanayama, 2021; Roballo & Delgado, 2019). Felt presence (FP) is the vivid experience of sensing another agent nearby without corroborating sensory evidence (Alderson-Day, 2016; Barnby & Bell, 2017). Systematic reviews indicate that FP occurs across a remarkably broad range of contexts and populations, from clinical neurological conditions to non-clinical samples in the general population (Alderson-Day, 2016; Barnby et al., 2023; Brederoo et al., 2024). This phenomenon has been well documented in neurological patients following temporoparietal lesions (Blanke et al., 2014), in healthy individuals during extreme stress and sensory deprivation (Geiger, 2009), during sleep paralysis (Cheyne & Girard, 2007), and in non-clinical community samples (Alderson-Day et al., 2023; Brederoo et al., 2024). Research on Parkinson's disease has also documented FP as a common minor hallucination (Fénelon et al., 2010). Additionally, FP can be reliably induced by electrical stimulation of the temporoparietal junction (Arzy et al., 2006, also see, Dary et al., 2023), implicating body-schema-related cortical areas in its generation. Because FP is also typically localised close to the body (see below), these findings suggest that FP may be closely related to mechanisms underlying the bodily representation of near-body space.

One framework that directly addresses these mechanisms is the theory of bodily selfconsciousness (BSC; Blanke, 2012). As articulated by Blanke and colleagues (Blanke, 2012; Lenggenhager et al., 2007), BSC refers to the integrated multisensory experience of selfidentification, self-location, and first-person perspective, grounded in the multisensory processing of peripersonal space (PPS) the zone immediately surrounding the body within which the body schema integrates information about nearby objects and agents (Rizzolatti et al., 1997; Serino, 2019).

Estimates of the functional boundary of PPS place the reaching space at approximately 60-80 cm from the body, a range consistent with the visual receptive fields of ventral premotor cortex (vPMC) neurons, which can extend up to about 1 m from the body (Serino, 2019). Broader interpersonal and social boundaries extend to roughly 120-180 cm (Serino, 2019; Teneggi et al., 2013). The precise boundary varies by individual and context, as PPS is technically a gradient operationalized via sigmoidal curve fitting rather than a fixed threshold (Serino, 2019). Notably, FP experiences are typically localized within or near this peripersonal boundary, most often behind or beside the perceiver (Alderson-Day et al., 2023). Experimental studies further support this spatial pattern: FP can be reliably induced through robot-controlled proprioceptive-tactile mismatches, which consistently produce the experience of an agent located in the posterior peripersonal space (Blanke et al., 2014), although the spontaneous reports from neurological and non-clinical samples (Alderson-Day et al., 2023; Brugger et al., 1996) suggest the posterior localization is a robust feature beyond the experimental setup. The question of whether childhood ICs share this phenomenology is theoretically motivated. First, the developmental period of peak IC prevalence coincides with the protracted maturation of PPS representations and BSC components. Children ages three to eight systematically overestimate reachability (Gabbard et al., 2007), and BSC components do not reach adult levels until approximately age 10-11 (Cowie et al., 2016; Gottwald et al., 2021). Recent virtual-reality work has further shown that, compared to adults, children embody artificial bodies more readily and are less constrained by visuomotor mismatches and reduced human-likeness (Weijs et al., 2021), suggesting that the bodily self is more plastic in this age range. This developmental plasticity may create favourable conditions for the incorporation of internally generated agent representations within near-body space. Second, if the same generative mechanisms underlie both phenomena, then a history of ICs should leave a detectable trace in adult propensity for FP experiences.

A further theoretical bridge is provided by predictive processing accounts. Within predictive processing frameworks (Friston, 2005 (Friston, , 2010;; Clark, 2013; Sterzer et al., 2018; Barnby et al., 2023), the brain continuously generates top-down predictions about the presence and location of social agents. This generative architecture termed the "Bayesian brain" by Friston (2010) maintains hierarchical models of the environment and updates them through prediction error minimization. FP may arise when this predictive mechanism becomes hyperactivated under conditions of ambiguous or degraded sensory input, paralleling the voluntary generation of sustained social-agent representations during childhood imaginative play (Taylor, 1999; Lillard, 2001). Consistent with this interpretation, the Social Deafferentation Hypothesis (Hoffman, 2007) proposes that reduced social input can trigger compensatory hyperactivation of socialrepresentational processes. These accounts collectively suggest that individual differences in how readily the brain generates social-agent representations may play a key role in the emergence of imaginary companions. Previous studies by Moriguchi and Shinohara (2012) and Moriguchi et al. (2019) bear on the mechanisms by which children represent imagined agents; the latter reports that imagined agents are perceptually represented by children but not by adults. The present account is compatible with either outcome, because it does not require that ICs be perceptually instantiated.

Given that, the hypotheses tested in the current study concern the spatial and perspectival organisation of internally generated agent representations within a developing bodily selfconsciousness framework, not the perceptual reality of the represented agent. We argue that a representation may be spatially anchored within peripersonal space and experienced from an embodied perspective without being perceptually instantiated. Recent work has begun to examine such individual differences by focusing on anthropomorphic attribution tendencies. Yamaguchi et al. (2023) found that anthropomorphic tendencies (the tendency to attribute human-like mental states to non-human entities), together with perceived stress, explained whether young adults currently had an imaginary companion. Within a predictive processing framework, elevated anthropomorphic tendencies can be interpreted as reflecting stronger prior expectations for agentive entities, thereby lowering the threshold for generating IC representations. This perspective links the IC phenomenon to variability in social-agent inference rather than to social deficit.

1.2 Prior Research on Imaginary Companions and Anomalous Experience

The question of whether childhood IC experience is continuous with adult presence-related phenomena is not new. A sustained programme of empirical research has already established that the two domains overlap. Laythe, Houran, and Little (2021) conducted a content analysis of naturalistic online accounts of childhood ICs and reported that companions attributed a ghostly character scored higher on a Rasch-scaled inventory of anomalous experiences associated with entity encounters. Little et al. (2021) extended this comparison in a quasi-quantitative analysis contrasting childhood IC accounts with ghostly-episode reports across multiple phenomenological dimensions, and proposed transliminality (i.e., the tendency for unconscious or preconscious material to cross into conscious awareness) as a candidate individual-difference mechanism common to both.

Two further studies examined the structure of IC phenomenology and its predictors. Lange et al. (2023) applied Rasch analysis to adults reporting childhood ICs and described a probabilistic hierarchy running from shallow, ostensibly adaptive contents to deep, relatively maladaptive contents. Drinkwater et al. (2024) Taken together, this research programme establishes that childhood IC phenomenology overlaps with anomalous and presence-related experience, that the overlap is graded rather than categorical, and that it reflects stable individual differences rather than pathology. The present study asks a question that follows from these findings: whether the overlap carries the specific spatial and perspectival signature that a bodily self-consciousness account predicts. That question has not been addressed for a reason that is methodological rather than conceptual. The prior work characterised IC phenomenology through coded narrative accounts and Rasch-scaled inventories, designs well suited to establishing that two classes of experience resemble one another but not to yielding spatial estimates that can be compared with an independently established boundary. The present design elicits distance estimates in centimetres along six body-centred axes together with a forced-choice perspectival judgement, permitting the peripersonal-extrapersonal distinction to be evaluated quantitatively rather than inferred descriptively. The present study is accordingly best understood as an independent conceptual replication and theoretical extension of this prior research programme, since it was conducted within a distinct theoretical framework (bodily self-consciousness and peripersonal space), with direct spatial and perspectival judgements rather than coded narratives or Rasch-scaled inventories.

1.3 The Present Study and Hypotheses

Within this framework, research on adult FP has established that FP experiences are typically localized within PPS (Alderson-Day et al., 2023), recalled from first-person perspective, and associated with hallucination-proneness rather than dissociation (Alderson-Day et al., 2023; Brederoo et al., 2024). Research on ICs has documented positive associations with theory of mind (Taylor & Carlson, 1997; Giménez-Dasí et al., 2016; Davis et al., 2023), and modest associations with dissociation in clinical samples (McLewin & Muller, 2006; Huolman & Peltonen, 2022) though whether such associations hold non-clinically remains open. Beyond theory of mind, IC experience has been linked to enhanced other-mind orientation and empathic capacities (Davis et al., 2014; Taylor et al., 2004), capacities that themselves draw on the ability to flexibly shift between embodied (1PP) and decentered (3PP) self-representations and that have been implicated in adaptive self-regulation, as in Solomon's paradox, where adopting a disembodied perspective improves reasoning about one's own dilemmas (Grossmann & Kross, 2014). Convergently, susceptibility to experimentally induced bodily illusions in adults an index of bodily-self plasticity correlates with trait empathy (Asai et al., 2011; Seiryte & Rusconi, 2015), supporting the view that flexible bodily self-representation scaffolds social cognition. Building on this foundation, a novel question now arises whether the documented overlap between IC phenomenology and anomalous or presence-related experience carries the specific spatial and perspectival signature that a bodily self-consciousness account predicts, and whether IC history predicts adult FP propensity as indexed by a standardised FP instrument. In the current study, the Dissociation Questionnaire (DIS-Q; Vanderlinden et al., 1993) was included as a discriminant measure, allowing us to test whether any association between IC status and FP propensity is specific rather than a reflection of general dissociative tendencies in a healthy sample. A lack of a group difference in dissociation however would not, on its own, show that this association is unique to FP. Whether IC history makes a larger difference to FP than to dissociation was examined in a post hoc comparison.

A bodily self-consciousness account makes testable predictions here: if ICs depend on the same mechanisms as the bodily self-consciousness, they should be felt near the body and experienced from a first-person point of view. More specifically, we tested three hypotheses. First, ICs should, as other bodily-self-related phenomena like FP experiences, be predominantly localized within PPS, the near-body region where multisensory signals are integrated to guide action and interaction with nearby agents. Second, interactions with ICs should be experienced, and to some degree also recalled, predominantly from a body-referenced perspective (first-person or mixed first-and third-person) rather than a decentred third-person perspective, consistent with the experiential organization of BSC. However, people usually recall their own past experiences from a first-person perspective (Nigro & Neisser, 1983; Rice & Rubin, 2009) and is therefore not, by itself, diagnostic of an FP-like phenomenology. The theoretically informative test is rather the conjunction of a predominantly body-referenced perspective (Hypothesis 2) with peripersonal spatial anchoring (Hypothesis 1) and elevated FP propensity (Hypothesis 3); together, this triad would be consistent with an embodied, BSC-anchored origin of IC representations, whereas any one component on its own would not be. Finally, if ICs and FP reflect related generative mechanisms for representing social agents and/or a more plastic bodily self-representation that more readily accommodates such imaginary agents within near-body space, individuals who reported childhood ICs should show a greater propensity for FP experiences in adulthood. We therefore examined whether retrospective reports of IC experiences exhibit these predicted spatial and perspectival characteristics and whether adults with a history of ICs display elevated FP propensity as measured by the Sensed Presence Questionnaire (SenPQ).

Accordingly, in the current study we tested the following three hypotheses. Hypothesis 1 (Peripersonal Anchoring) predicted that retrospectively reported IC locations would fall predominantly within peripersonal space, that is, that most reported locations would lie at 70 cm or less from the body. Because peripersonal space is a gradient rather than a fixed limit, we also examined whether this result held at other boundaries. Hypothesis 2 (Embodied Perspective) predicted that IC interactions would be reported predominantly from a body-referenced visual perspective (first-person or mixed first-and third-person) rather than from a decentred third-person perspective. Hypothesis 3 (Continuity of Agent Propensity) predicted that adults reporting a history of childhood ICs would show higher FP propensity, as indexed by the SenPQ, than adults reporting no such history.

2. Method

>Method

2.1 Participants

A total of 231 adults were recruited online from İzmir University of Economics. All participants provided informed consent electronically before completing the survey. Forty-six participants (19.9%) reporting a current or previous psychiatric or neurological diagnosis were excluded following standard practice in non-clinical cognitive research (Alderson-Day et al., 2023; Brederoo et al., 2024). Excluded diagnoses included depression (n = 12), anxiety disorders (n = 10), ADHD (n = 5), bipolar disorder (n = 3), dissociative identity disorder (n = 1), epilepsy (n = 1), and multiple sclerosis (n = 1), among others. Participants who were excluded due to psychiatric or neurological conditions showed slightly higher dissociation scores (DIS-Q; M = 2.68, SD = 0.45) than the healthy sample (M = 2.56, SD = 0.38), although this difference was not significant, t(229) = 1.88, p = .062. They also reported slightly higher FP scores on the Sensed Presence Questionnaire (SenPQ; excluded: M = 1.58, SD = 0.72; healthy: M = 1.43, SD = 0.57), but this difference was not statistically significant (p = .139). The prevalence of imaginary companions was 19.6% among excluded and 24.3% among retained participants. The resulting sample (N = 185) comprised 152 women (82.2%), 31 men (16.8%), and 2 participants of other/unspecified gender (1.1%). Mean age was 23.91 years (SD = 6.78, range 18-55). Most (81.6%) were undergraduate students. Of the 185 retained participants, 45 (24.3%) were IC-positive and 140 (75.7%) IC-negative. The groups did not differ significantly on gender, age, or education (Table 1). Ethics approval: B.30.2. IEU.05.05-020-165.

2.2 Measures

The present study employed three primary instruments selected to capture the core constructs relevant to the hypothesized relationship between childhood IC experiences and adult FP propensity. The selection of measures was guided by the theoretical framework linking ICs to BSC and social-agent representation, and by the need to dissociate FP propensity from general dissociative tendencies.

2.2.1 IC Questionnaire (IC-Q).

IC-positive participants completed a 39-item questionnaire designed to comprehensively assess the phenomenology of childhood IC experiences. The questionnaire covers IC appearance, size, sensory modality, duration of the relationship, age of onset and disappearance, mimicry behaviors, tactile interaction, and the presence of secret language. Item content was derived from established protocols in the IC literature (Taylor, 1999; Hoff, 2004). The descriptive item set follows the interview-based tradition developed by Taylor and colleagues for characterising companion identity, appearance, modality and interaction (Taylor, 1999; Taylor & Aguiar, 2024), and the adult retrospective items follow the survey approach of Fernyhough et al. (2019); the spatial localisation and perspectival items are additions specific to the present hypotheses. The IC-Q was written in Turkish for the present study, with content adapted from these English-language sources rather than translated from an existing instrument; the English version in Appendix A is a reader's translation that has not been validated for administration, and no independent psychometric evidence is available for either version.

Critically, the IC-Q included dedicated sections assessing spatial localization and visual perspective, which served as the primary outcome variables for Hypotheses 1 and 2, respectively (Section 3.2, which reports the spatial localization results, and Section 3.3, which reports the visual perspective results). In the spatial localization section, IC-positive participants rated the frequency with which their IC appeared in each of six spatial directions (front, behind, below, above, right, left) using a 7-point scale (1 = never,7 = very often), and estimated the typical distance (in centimetres) at which the IC was experienced for each direction. Each distance item immediately followed the corresponding frequency item and asked only for a value in centimetres ("please state in centimetres"; original Turkish wording in Appendix B); participants received no instruction about what to enter for a direction in which the companion had never appeared, and the form offered no not-applicable option (Section 2.4 describes how such entries were classified).

Each direction was illustrated by a card showing a schematic figure beside a distance scale marked at 1, 20, 150, 300, and 500 cm; the cards are included in the data deposit. For the visual perspective section (Item 38), participants chose among four fixed options and an open "other" field: (a) perception also from the companion's viewpoint, (b) perception solely from one's own viewpoint, (c) do not remember, (d) both, or (e) other, with a free-text description. For analysis, option (b) was coded as first-person, options (a) and (d) as mixed, and (c) as do not remember; free-text responses describing exclusively decentred viewpoints were coded as third-person. Options (a), (b) and (d) together constitute the body-referenced category. The item offered no fixed option for an exclusively decentred (third-person) perspective, which could be reported only through the freetext field. It was accompanied by two illustrative cards depicting options (a) and (b), whose headings were printed inverted relative to the coding convention: the card for option (a) was headed "first-person perspective" and the card for option (b) "third-person perspective" (original Turkish headings in Appendix B). The option texts themselves do not refer to the headings. Table 2 lists each option, in English translation, with its analytic category and its count; the original Turkish wording of each option is given in Appendix B, and the consequences of the heading error for Hypothesis 2 are analysed in Section 3.3. Replications should not reuse the item as administered: a revised version should correct the card headings and add a fixed option, with its own card, for an exclusively decentred perspective. The administered version and a version with corrected headings are included in the data deposit. These items were included to enable direct tests of whether IC experiences are spatially anchored within the peripersonal boundary (approximately 60-80 cm; Serino, 2019) and recalled from an embodied, body-centered perspective. Two examples, translated from the Turkish, illustrate the two item types most consequential for the hypotheses: "How often did you feel your imaginary companion in front of you, relative to your body?" (1 = I never felt it,7 = I felt it very often) and "At what distance in front of you, relative to your body, did you feel your imaginary companion?" (please state in centimetres).

The IC-Q applied the narrower definitional criterion of an invisible companion: the screening item asked about a companion that was not visible to other people, and personified objects were not counted as ICs on that basis alone. Two IC-positive participants nevertheless reported that the companion was visible to other people (Item 12), and 18 that it also existed as a toy or object (Item 13). Both were retained; excluding the two leaves all three confirmatory results unchanged in direction and significance. Free-text responses to the "other" field of Item 38 were coded by a single rater (the first author) against the mapping stated above; because only one rater coded these responses, no inter-rater agreement coefficient is available, and this is noted as a limitation. Because the IC-Q indexes heterogeneous descriptive features of IC phenomenology rather than a unidimensional latent construct, internal-consistency coefficients are not reported for this instrument and would not be interpretable. The full IC-Q is provided in English translation in Appendix A and in the original Turkish as administered in Appendix B.

2.2.2 Sensed Presence Questionnaire (SenPQ).

FP propensity was assessed using the SenPQ developed by Barnby and Bell (2017). The SenPQ is a 16-item self-report measure designed to assess the frequency with which individuals experience the sensation that another entity or agent is present despite the absence of clear sensory evidence. Items are rated on a 5point Likert scale ranging from 1 (Never) to 5 (Always). In the original psychometric validation study (N = 191), the SenPQ demonstrated excellent internal consistency (Cronbach's α = .951).

Exploratory principal components analysis revealed a two-factor structure: the first factor, interpreted as reflecting benign sensed presence experiences (Items 3, 5, 6, 8, 11, 12, 13, 15), explained 52.28% of the variance; the second factor, interpreted as reflecting malign sensed presence experiences (Items 1, 2, 4, 9, 10, 14, 16), explained an additional 7.66% of the variance.

Item 7 ("When I have visited specific locations, I felt I was in the presence of an unseen being or beings") was excluded from the factor scoring because it showed substantive cross-loading on both factors (Barnby & Bell, 2017). Accordingly, a 15-item factor-based scoring approach was adopted.

Factor scores were computed as the sum of items loading on each factor (F1 Benign: 8 items, range 8-40; F2 Malign: 7 items, range , and the overall SenPQ total score represents the sum of these 15 items (range 15-75). Per-item means are additionally reported for interpretive comparison. In the present study, a Turkish-adapted version of the SenPQ was administered. The provenance of this adaptation is stated in the Limitations, together with its implications for replication. Internal consistency in the current sample was high for the 15-item total (α = .911), F1 Benign (α = .859), and F2 Malign (α = .848). The original 16-item Cronbach's α was .918. The scoring choice is not consequential: the 16-item and 15-item solutions yield closely comparable group differences (d = 0.68 vs. d = 0.66), a comparison recomputed from the item-level responses included in the deposited dataset. The SenPQ was administered with a standard preamble instructing participants to report only genuinely felt or perceived presences, to exclude experiences occurring under the influence of recreational drugs, and to consider only the preceding one-month period. It is important to note that because all participants were adults, the one-month window means that responses index current FP propensity in adulthood rather than lifetime or retrospective childhood experience (Appendix C).

2.2.3 Dissociation Questionnaire (DIS-Q).

Dissociative experiences were assessed using the DIS-Q (Vanderlinden et al., 1993), a widely used self-report instrument designed to measure dissociative phenomena in both clinical and non-clinical populations. The questionnaire consists of 63 items rated on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (Not at all) to 5 (Extremely). The instrument is described by its authors as spanning four dimensions of dissociation identity confusion, loss of control, amnesia, and absorption but only the DIS-Q total score was computed and analysed in the present study. Subscale scores were not derived, and no subscale reliability coefficients are therefore reported. The present study used the Turkish adaptation of the DIS-Q developed by Şar et al. (1998), which demonstrated excellent reliability (α = .98). In the current sample, the DIS-Q showed good internal consistency (Cronbach's α = .870).

2.3 Procedure

The study was administered online via Google Forms. After providing informed consent 2.4.1 Sample Size and Software: No a priori power analysis was conducted; sample size was determined by the size of the participant pool available during the recruitment window of a single semester period (3 months).

2.4 Statistical Analysis

We therefore report a sensitivity analysis (two-tailed alpha = .05, power = .80), following the approach recommended for fixed-N designs (Lakens, 2022), which indicates that the achieved sample (IC+ n = 45; IC-n = 140) was sensitive to between-group effects of Cohen's d ≥ 0.48. For Hypothesis 2, the exact binomial test (two-sided, n = 45) had 75% power to detect a true proportion of 70% against a 50% null. Power reached 80% when the true proportion was about 71%. The study was not powered to detect small differences in dissociation: the design had 80% power only for differences of d ≥ 0.48, so the conclusion from the DIS-Q comparison on its own is limited to excluding group differences larger than about half a standard deviation (Section 3.5, which reports the DIS-Q comparison by IC status).

All statistical analyses were conducted in Python 3.12 using SciPy, pandas, NumPy, statsmodels (logistic regression, variance inflation factors, false-discovery-rate adjustment, generalised estimating equations). SenPQ scores were computed using the 15-item factor-based scoring (excluding Item 7 due to cross-loading), with factor scores as sums and per-item means reported for interpretive comparison.

2.4.2 Spatial Localization of ICs (Hypothesis 1): In order to test the prediction that ICs would be localized within PPS, spatial distance data were categorized dichotomously using the 70 cm boundary as the operational criterion for the peripersonal-extrapersonal distinction. This value corresponds to the midpoint of the 60-80 cm range converged upon in the adult PPS literature (Ferri et al., 2015; Longo & Lourenco, 2007; Serino, 2019). This range is consistent with neurophysiological evidence from the macaque, in which the visual receptive fields of ventral premotor cortex neurons are anchored to a body part and extend from about 5 cm up to 1 m from it (Serino, 2019). Human studies further show that the PPS boundary depends on the body part tested, lying at approximately 30-45 cm for the hand, 50-60 cm for the face, and 70-80 cm for the trunk (Serino, 2019). Because a companion felt near the body is plausibly located with respect to the body as a whole rather than to a single limb, the trunk-centred boundary provides the most direct empirical basis for the present criterion, and the 70 cm value lies at its lower limit. We adopted the midpoint of the 60-80 cm range, recognising that PPS is properly modelled as a sigmoidal gradient rather than a hard threshold (Serino, 2019). The distance items had no "not applicable" option (Section 2.2.1, which describes the questionnaire items). A distance entry therefore does not show on its own that the companion appeared in that direction. We therefore used the frequency rating given just before each distance item to decide whether the companion had appeared in that direction. A direction counted as an occurrence if it was rated 2 or higher on the 1-7 scale (1 = never). Distance entries for directions rated 1 were treated as non-occurrences, whatever their value. For occurring directions, every entry was kept, including 0 cm. Each participant gave several reports, so the proportion of reports at or within 70 cm was tested against .50 with a generalised estimating equation (Liang & Zeger, 1986). Because only 41 participants contributed occurrence reports, we also used a bias-reduced covariance as a small-sample check (Mancl & DeRouen, 2001).

In addition, to test whether the result also held at the participant level, a sign test was applied to each participant's median distance. We used each participant's median rather than the grand mean for two reasons. Each participant gave several distance estimates (one per direction), and the median is more robust to the skewed distributions and extreme values common in distance estimation tasks. To test the possibility that the result depended on the summary measure, a

Wilcoxon signed-rank test also compared participant medians with 70 cm. However, the proportion of reports within the boundary nevertheless served as the primary outcome, for three reasons. First, Hypothesis 1 concerns this proportion directly, so testing it gives a more exact answer to the question the hypothesis asks. Second, with medians as skewed as these, the signedrank test addresses the pseudo-median rather than the median. Third, the proportion can be computed at any boundary, so the conclusion does not rest on the 70 cm value alone, and Table D.1 shows how far the result generalises to other boundaries. The proportion was adopted as the primary outcome after we had seen that the Wilcoxon test was not significant once 0-cm entries were removed; the occurrence rule and the clustered model were then written down before distance entries were cross-tabulated with frequency ratings.

Follow-up analyses, reported in Appendix D, examined how far the Hypothesis 1 result depends on these analytic choices. Because the 70 cm criterion is an adult value and children's reaching space is shorter, the test was repeated at narrower or larger boundaries. For comparison, we also report an analysis that treated every distance entry, including 0 cm, as a location. Table D.1 gives the result under the other codings and boundaries. Figure 2 summarises the per-axis values on a body-centred schematic. The results of these analyses are reported in Section 3.2, which describes the spatial localization of ICs.

2.4.3 Visual Perspective (Hypothesis 2): A report was classed as body-referenced if the participant chose either the first-person option or a mixed first-and third-person option, because both perspectives are anchored to the body. For Hypothesis 2, an exact binomial test compared the proportion of body-referenced reports with 50%. We used 50% because "predominantly" in Hypothesis 2 means "more than half". It is not a chance level, because three of the four fixed options were body-referenced, so even participants who answered at random would be expected to give mostly body-referenced answers. The proportion of first-person reports is described but not tested. A test against 25% would assume that all four options were equally likely, and the item was not designed that way.

Because the item offered no fixed third-person option, a participant who meant to report a third-person perspective may have chosen a body-referenced option by mistake. In order to test for this possibility, we calculated how many body-referenced answers would have to be such mistakes for the test to lose significance. The results are reported in Section 3.3, which describes the visual perspective of IC interactions.

2.4.4 SenPQ and Dissociation Scores by IC Status (Hypothesis 3):To examine differences

in FP propensity between individuals with and without IC history, independent-samples t tests were conducted on SenPQ scores. Levene's test (median-centred) indicated unequal variances for all three SenPQ comparisons (total, W = 10.63, p = .001; F1, W = 13.48, p < .001; F2, W = 4.91, p = .028), so Welch's t test is reported throughout, with the corresponding Student's t values given in the table note for comparability. Mean differences are reported with 95% confidence intervals computed under the same Welch model as the test statistic. Effect sizes are reported as Cohen's d using the pooled standard deviation, with 95% confidence intervals derived from the standard normal approximation. Assumptions of normality for dissociation scores were evaluated using the Shapiro-Wilk test, which did not indicate departure from normality in either group (IC+: p = .496; IC-: p = .313).

To evaluate the discriminant expectation, we compared the size of the IC-related group difference on the SenPQ with that on the DIS-Q in the same participants, d(SenPQ) -d(DIS-Q).

Its 95% percentile confidence interval was obtained from a bootstrap stratified by IC status (10,000 resamples). This comparison was specified after both group differences were known, so it is reported as post hoc. Two checks accompany it. The first tested whether the point-biserial correlations of IC status with the two measures differed, taking into account that both were computed in the same participants (Williams's t; Steiger, 1980). The second, used because of the floor in the SenPQ distribution, compared the two measures on a rank-based metric, the area under the ROC curve (AUC), with a bootstrap confidence interval.

Only five IC-positive participants were men. As a follow-up analysis, the SenPQ comparison was therefore repeated among women alone and with gender entered as a covariate (ordinary least squares with HC3 standard errors). The results are reported in Section 3.4, which compares SenPQ scores by IC status, and Section 3.5, which compares dissociation scores by IC status.

2.4.5 Exploratory Analyses: In addition to the primary hypothesis tests, exploratory analyses were conducted to further examine relationships among variables. For these, the family of exploratory tests was defined in advance of adjustment as the fourteen inferential tests reported in Sections 3.6.1 to 3.6.4, and Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction was applied across that family; adjusted values are reported as q throughout to distinguish them from uncorrected p values. A test is described as significant after adjustment when q < .05, and a test with p ≥ .05 is described as not significant. Rank-based (Spearman) coefficients are reported as robustness checks on Pearson tests already in the family and are not separate members of it.

As a follow-up, Figure D.1 (Appendix D) displays the association between behind-axis frequency ratings and SenPQ scores within the IC-positive subsample. The figure reports the directional frequency analyses. All exploratory results are reported in Section 3.6.

3. Results

>Results

3.1 IC Characteristics

Five of the 45 IC-positive participants (11.1%) reported ongoing contact with their companion at the time of the study, and 40 (88.9%) did not. As a share of the whole sample (5 of 185, 2.7%), current contact was less common than in Davis et al. (2026), where 11% of adults reported a current imaginary companion, and Fernyhough et al. (2019), where the figure was 7%; the samples and question wording differ.

Of the IC-positive participants (n = 45), 60.0% (n = 27) reported having siblings during childhood, whereas 40.0% (n = 18) were only children.

All 27 participants with siblings answered the sibling-IC item, and none reported that a sibling had had an imaginary companion (70.4%, n = 19, "don't know"; 29.6%, n = 8, "no"). Six participants without siblings also answered the item and are not counted here. Household pet ownership during childhood was likewise uncommon (8.9%, n = 4). The IC-Q did not offer "lack of an animal companion" as a reason for IC creation; the item recorded only whether a pet was present in the household, and no inference about motivation is drawn from it here. Eighteen participants (40.0%) reported that the companion also existed as a real toy or object (Item 13); this variable is used as a robustness check on the spatial findings (Section 3.2).

Among IC-positive participants who reported ages (onset n = 32; disappearance n = 33; duration n = 35), the mean age of IC onset was 6.56 years (SD = 3.21, Mdn = 5.0, range 3-17). ICs had typically disappeared by a mean age of 10.06 years (SD = 4.25, Mdn = 8.0), with a mean relationship duration of 28.5 months (SD = 17.3).

Entries of 0 (two for onset, four for disappearance) were treated as missing; with them excluded, no participant reported a disappearance age earlier than the onset age. The median number of ICs reported was 1.0 (M = 1.44). The majority of ICs were described as child-like (88.6%) and smaller than the participant (68.9%). With respect to phenomenological form, of 42 codable responses (3 cases coded outside the response set were treated as missing), 71.4% (n = 30) described their IC as animal-like, 19.0% (n = 8) as monster-like, 4.8% (n = 2) as human-like, and 4.8% (n = 2) as "other"; no participant endorsed the toy option at this item. Combined, animal and monster forms accounted for 90.5% of codable responses (38 of 42). All form percentages are computed on the 42 codable responses. Naming responses showed a similarly informative distribution: although all 45 participants provided a free-text response to the name item, 31.1% (n = 14) reported that they no longer remembered the IC's name and an additional 13.3% (n = 6) reported that the IC had no name; among the 25 named companions, "Ayşe" was the only name appearing more than once (n = 3). The high "don't remember" rate (approximately 31%) is itself theoretically relevant for the present retrospective design and is consistent with substantial recall attenuation for fine-grained identifying details across the roughly 13-to 16-year interval between IC age and report (see Limitations). Most participants reported conversing with their IC (88.9%), whereas relatively few reported special language (8.9%), tactile interaction (11.1%), or olfactory features (4.5%).

Behavioral mirroring by the IC was reported at moderate rates: 24.4% (n = 11) reported that their IC imitated the participant's movements, and 22.2% (n = 10) reported imitation of posture (one further response was recorded as "1" rather than Yes or No and was not counted; counting it as yes gives 24.4%, n = 11). Together with the dominant conversing rate, these data indicate that approximately one in four ICs was experienced as engaging in observable, body-referenced reciprocal behavior. With respect to visual perceptual modality (IC-Q Item 16; n = 45), 26.7% of participants (n = 12) chose "Neither", describing a companion that was neither seen nor sensed in the environment; because this option does not place the companion on the sensed-visible dimension, these participants were excluded from modality-specific analyses. Among the 33 participants who provided a valid response, the distribution was approximately even between FPlike and visually explicit modes: 39.4% (n = 13) described their IC as "sensed like a ghost" without visual content, whereas 39.4% (n = 13) as physically visible, and 21.2% (n = 7) as both.

3.2 Spatial Localization of ICs

The first hypothesis predicted that childhood imaginary companions would be predominantly localized within peripersonal space (PPS), the near-body zone within which the brain integrates multisensory information for action and body-schema maintenance. As outlined above, empirical estimates place the functional PPS boundary at approximately 60-80 cm; we therefore adopted 70 cm, the midpoint of that range, as the operational criterion. The 70 cm value is this study's operational criterion and is not claimed to be a universal biological boundary.

Each IC-positive participant (n = 45) rated how often the companion had appeared in each of six directions and gave a distance estimate for each direction, yielding 270 frequency ratings and 255 distance entries (15 distance items were left blank by 7 participants). Of the 255 distance entries, 141 were given for directions that the participant had rated as never occupied by the companion, including 90 of the 92 entries of 0 cm, 15 of the 29 entries of 1 cm and 36 other values, 17 of them 500 cm, the largest value on the printed scale (Table D.1). Under the occurrence rule (Section 2.4), 114 distance entries from 41 participants described directions in which the companion had appeared; three participants rated every direction as never, and one participant who reported occurrences left the corresponding distance items blank. Occurrence reports were rightskewed and coarse (Mdn = 20 cm, IQR = 20-150 cm; M = 73.43 cm, SD = 99.79): 72 of 114 were 30 cm or less, none fell between 50 and 80 cm, 38 exceeded 80 cm, and 82 (71.9%) coincided with a mark on the printed scale (1, 20, 150, 300, or 500 cm). The 70 cm boundary therefore effectively separated the two nearest scale marks from the farther ones, and because no occurrence report fell between 50 and 80 cm, every boundary within the 60-80 cm range cited in the peripersonal space literature classifies every report identically.

Under the occurrence rule, 76 of 114 reports (66.7%) fell at or within 70 cm. The clustered estimate of this proportion was .64, 95% CI [.51, .75], significantly above .50 (GEE, z = 2.04, p = .042); with the bias-reduced covariance the interval was [.50, .75] (z = 1.99, p = .047), and, referred to a t distribution with 40 degrees of freedom, p = .054. The participant-level sign test gave a similar result (28 of 41 participants with a median at or within 70 cm, 68.3%, p = .028), whereas the Wilcoxon signed-rank test on per-participant medians was not significant (W = 388.0, p = .767). In follow-up post hoc tests, we repeated the analysis at different distances and under different codings, and these results are reported in Appendix D (Table D.1). The result depended on these analytic choices. The result was not significant at a 30-40 cm boundary, but it was significant at boundaries of 50 cm or more and under a stricter occurrence rule (directions rated 3 or higher). It was no longer significant when the 14 entries of exactly 1 cm for occurring directions were also treated as non-occurrences, a stress test whose rationale is given in the note to Table D.1. Treating every entry, including 0 cm, as a location gave a higher proportion (Table D.1); these figures are retained for comparison only, because they count entries for directions in which the companion never appeared as near-body locations. Hypothesis 1 was therefore moderately supported: companions were more often within than beyond 70 cm, but the margin was small and depended on analytic choices.

The per-axis pattern (Figure 1A; Figure 2) is descriptive. Lateral reports were mostly within 70 cm (left 20 of 28, 71.4%; right 21 of 30, 70.0%), whereas frontal reports were evenly divided (16 of 31, 51.6%; Mdn = 30 cm); reports behind the body were few (11 of 15 within 70 cm), and vertical occurrence reports rarer still (above 6, below 4). A post hoc clustered contrast of frontal with lateral (left and right) reports, from a GEE fitted to those reports alone, gave p = .007 (p = .005 within the model containing all directions), but an omnibus Wald test across five direction levels (front, behind, left, right, vertical combined) was not significant, χ²(4) = 8.13, p = .087 and differences among directions were not part of the hypotheses, so, as with the pairwise comparison in Section 3.6.4, the contrast is not interpreted. In the all-entry coding, the above and below axes had appeared the most peripersonal (83.7% each, Mdn = 0 cm) only because most of their entries were non-occurrences. The horizontal-plane dominance figure of 97.8% was derived from the frequency ratings, as the proportion of participants whose highest horizontal rating was at least as high as their highest vertical rating, and it counted as horizontal-dominant, through ties, three participants who rated every direction as never. Of the 42 participants who rated their companion as present in at least one direction, 39 (92.9%) gave a horizontal direction a higher rating than either vertical direction, 2 rated them equally and 1 rated a vertical direction higher; none reported vertical occurrences only, and 104 of the 114 occurrence reports (91.2%) were on horizontal axes (Figure 2). Because four horizontal directions are compared with two vertical ones, some horizontal advantage is expected by construction; the more telling figure is that only 9 of 45 participants reported any vertical occurrence, against 42 who reported a horizontal one.

A robustness check addressed companions that also existed as a real toy or object (Item 13; 18 of 45 participants), since such a companion could be spatially anchored by the object rather than by peripersonal representation. Excluding these participants left the estimate unchanged under the occurrence rule (44 of 66 reports, 66.7%; clustered estimate .64), although with 24 contributing participants it was not significant (95% CI [.46, .79], z = 1.58, p = .114). Figure 1 occurrence reports only, that is, distance entries for directions rated 2 or higher on the frequency scale (upper, darker bar of each pair; primary analysis, 114 reports), and all distance entries, including entries for directions rated as never occupied (lower, paler bar; 255 entries). Counts are given beside each bar; error bars are 95% Wilson score intervals (each participant contributes at most one report per axis); the dashed line marks 50%. Panel B shows mean frequency ratings (±SEM) across the six directions (1 = never,7 = very often); all 45 participants rated every direction. The all-entry ns (front 43, behind 43, left 42, right 41, above 43, below 43) are below 45 because some distance items were left unanswered. and vertical occurrence reports were few.

3.3 Visual Perspective

Of the 45 IC-positive participants, 25 (55.6%) chose the option describing perception solely from their own viewpoint (first-person), 15 (33.3%) chose one of the two options describing perception from both viewpoints (mixed), four (8.9%) described an exclusively decentred viewpoint in the free-text field (third-person), and one (2.2%) did not remember (Table 2, Figure 3).

Combining first-person and mixed responses, 40 of 45 participants (88.9%, 95% CI [75.9, 96.3]) reported a body-referenced perspective, significantly more than half (exact binomial p < .001); excluding the participant who did not remember gave 40 of 44 (90.9%). Because misselection between the first-person and mixed options cannot be recovered (see below), the firstperson count is reported but not interpreted. Three features of the item bear on these figures (Section 2.2.1). First, the headings of the two illustrative cards were inverted. Because both affected options, like option (d), lie within the body-referenced category, mis-selection between them could shift responses between the firstperson and mixed categories but could not move a response into or out of the body-referenced category. The first-person proportion is therefore not interpretable as an estimate, whereas the inversion could not have raised the body-referenced proportion. Second, the item offered no fixed third-person option, so a participant who wished to report a decentred perspective could only select a body-referenced option or describe that perspective in the free-text field, and the body-referenced proportion may therefore be inflated. The binomial test would lose significance if 11 or more of the 40 body-referenced responses were misrouted third-person reports, and body-referenced reports would cease to be a majority if 18 or more were. The data cannot estimate the misrouting rate. Third, three of the four fixed options were body-referenced, so a body-referenced majority would be expected even from participants responding without regard to content. Hypothesis 2 was therefore supported, but only weakly.

3.5 Dissociative Tendencies by IC Status

IC-positive participants (M = 2.59, SD = 0.35) did not differ significantly from IC-negative participants (M = 2.55, SD = 0.39) on DIS-Q total scores; the mean difference was 0.04, 95% CI [-0.08, 0.16], Welch's t(82.5) = 0.71, p = .478, Cohen's d = 0.12, 95% CI [-0.22, 0.45]. Levene's test was not significant for this comparison (W = 1.63, p = .203); Student's t(183) = 0.67, p = .502.

The confidence interval for d excludes a difference larger than about half a standard deviation but not a small one, so the conclusion from this comparison is limited to excluding differences of that size. The discriminant expectation was therefore evaluated comparatively, in an analysis specified after both group differences were known and reported as post hoc. The IC-related difference was larger on the SenPQ than on the DIS-Q, d(SenPQ) -d(DIS-Q) = 0.55, 95% CI [0.07, 1.03] (stratified bootstrap), and the corresponding point-biserial correlations differed (.27 vs .05;

Williams's t(182) = 2.39, p = .018). On a rank-based metric, appropriate given the floor in the SenPQ distribution, the difference was in the same direction but its interval included zero (AUC .66 vs .53; difference .13, 95% CI [-.01, .26]). The two measures were only weakly related in the full sample, and the Pearson and Spearman estimates of that relation differ in sign (r = .14, 95% CI [.00, .28], p = .050; ρ = -.04, p = .590), a divergence we attribute to the floor in the SenPQ distribution; on either estimate the two constructs share little variance, which is the premise of the comparison.

3.6 Exploratory Analyses

Analyses in this section are exploratory. The family for multiplicity adjustment was defined as the fourteen inferential tests reported in Sections 3.6.1 to 3.6.4. Uncorrected p values are reported alongside Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted values, denoted q, and no exploratory result is treated as confirmatory. Only two tests in this family were significant before adjustment: the SenPQ predictor in the logistic regression (p = .002), which remained significant after adjustment (q = .029), and the correlation between age and DIS-Q scores (p = .036), which did not (q = .119).

None of the other twelve tests was significant (all p ≥ .05; all q ≥ .119). Adjusted values are sensitive to how the family is delimited, and the family used here is stated so that readers can Malign and the three directional regression models (Section 3.6.3); and the two Kruskal-Wallis tests (Section 3.6.4). Other coefficients reported in these sections, including the remaining sixteen directional correlations, are descriptive or robustness checks and are not adjusted. Had all eighteen directional correlations been included (30 tests), the q value for the SenPQ predictor would have been .063. All exploratory findings, including the one that remained significant after adjustment, are treated as hypothesis-generating.

3.6.1 Logistic Regression:

Gender and age were entered as demographic covariates; neither was significant. In Step 2, DIS-Q and SenPQ (15-item per-item mean) scores were added, yielding a significant improvement in model fit, Δχ²(2) = 10.43, p = .005. The full model was significant, χ²(4) = 14.15, p = .007, McFadden pseudo-R² = .069, Nagelkerke R² = .110. SenPQ was the sole significant predictor (B = 0.91, SE = 0.30, OR = 2.49, 95% CI [1.39, 4.45], Wald χ²(1) = 9.47, p = .002; equivalently z = 3.08), whereas DIS-Q (χ²(1) = 0.01, p = .903), gender (χ²(1) = 0.85, p = .356), and age (χ²(1) = 0.65, p = .421) were not significant. This result remained significant after Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment across the exploratory family (q = .029); no other exploratory test was significant after adjustment.
