Full model: χ²(4) = 14.15, p = .007; McFadden pseudo-R² = .069; Cox-Snell R² = .074; Nagelkerke R² = .110. All variance inflation factors were below 1.1. The SenPQ effect remained significant after Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment across the exploratory analysis (q = .029).

3.6.2 Correlations:

IC status was significantly correlated with SenPQ (r = .27, p < .001) but not with DIS-Q (r = .05), gender (r = .10), or age (r = -.10).

The SenPQ-DIS-Q correlation was weak and its sign depended on the estimator (Section 3.5). Age showed a small negative correlation with DIS-Q (r = -.15, p = .036), which was not significant after adjustment (q = .119).

Pearson and Spearman estimates led to the same conclusion for every pair except three: they differed in sign for SenPQ-DIS-Q (Section 3.5), and in significance for gender-SenPQ (r = .14, 95% CI [-.01, .28], p = .059; ρ = .19, p = .011) and for age-DIS-Q (r = -.15, p = .036; ρ = -.14, p = .052). The full matrix, with Pearson coefficients below the diagonal and Spearman coefficients above it, is presented in Table 5.

3.6.3 Directional Frequency as a Predictor of FP Proneness Within IC+ Participants:

To examine whether specific spatial aspects of IC localization were differentially associated with adult FP proneness, bivariate correlations and simultaneous multiple regression analyses were conducted within the IC-positive subsample (n = 45). Six directional frequency ratings (Front, Behind, Below, Above, Right, Left; each rated 1-7) served as predictors, and three SenPQ scores served as dependent variables: SenPQ Total (15-item), Factor 1 Benign, and Factor 2 Malign. All 45 participants rated every direction, so each analysis is based on n = 45; the distance estimates, which do not enter these analyses, were available for 41 to 43 participants per direction.

At the bivariate level, none of the six directional frequencies was significantly associated with any SenPQ score. The largest coefficients involved behind-axis frequency (SenPQ Total r = .28, p = .065, q = .119; F1 Benign r = .25, p = .104; F2 Malign r = .29, p = .051, q = .119), none of which was significant before or after adjustment. The Spearman coefficient for F2 Malign, computed as a robustness check and not itself a member of the family, was ρ = .31 (unadjusted p = .037); because the corresponding Pearson test was not significant, it is not interpreted. For the other five directions, all |r| < .17 and all ps > .27. Differences among the six coefficients were not tested, and with n = 45 the study was not powered to detect them. These associations are displayed

Three multiple regression models (predicting SenPQ Total, Benign, and Malign scores) were estimated with all six directional frequencies entered as predictors.

No multicollinearity concerns were identified (all VIFs < 2.2), although Right and Left were substantially correlated (r = .68), as expected given their shared horizontal plane. None of the overall models reached statistical significance. For SenPQ Total, R² = .161, F(6, 38) = 1.22, p = .319. For F1 Benign, R² = .128, F(6, 38) = 0.93, p = .483. For F2 Malign, R² = .188, F(6, 38) = 1.47, p = .216.

3.6.4 Perceptual Modality Within IC+ Participants:

To explore whether the perceptual quality of the IC experience moderated FP proneness, participants were categorized by IC16 responses indicating whether their IC was experienced as "sensed like a ghost" (non-visual; n = 13), "physically visible" (visual; n = 13), or "both" (n = 7). The twelve participants who chose "Neither" were excluded from modality-specific analyses (Section 3.1, which reports the Item 16 response distribution).

SenPQ Total scores were lowest in the sensed group and highest in the both group: sensed/ghost (M = 20.85, SD = 6.24), visible (M = 27.46, SD = 13.36), and both (M = 34.43, SD = 12.87).

A Kruskal-Wallis test indicated that this between-group difference was not significant, H(2) = 5.56, p = .062. Pairwise Mann-Whitney U tests, reported for completeness, gave U = 17.0, p = .026 for the sensed versus both comparison, U = 57.0, p = .165 for sensed versus visible, and U = 31.0, p = .267 for visible versus both. Given the small subgroup sizes (ns = 13, 13, 7), these results are reported as exploratory only: the omnibus test was not significant before or after adjustment across the exploratory family (q = .119), and the pairwise comparison, which follows a non-significant omnibus test and is not part of the declared fourteen-test family, is not interpreted.

An additional exploratory analysis examined whether IC modality was associated with the spatial localization profile. Front frequency ratings did not differ significantly across modality groups, H(2) = 5.38, p = .068. The sensed/ghost group reported the highest frontal frequency (M = 4.00, SD = 1.53), followed by the visible group (M = 3.46, SD = 1.85) and both group (M = 2.29, SD = 0.76). This difference was not significant before or after adjustment (q = .119) and is not interpreted further.

4. Discussion

The present study is best understood as an independent conceptual replication and theoretical extension of prior work linking childhood imaginary companions to anomalous and presence-related experience (Drinkwater et al., 2024; Lange et al., 2023; Laythe et al., 2021; Little et al., 2021). Its main confirmatory result is that adults who report a childhood IC score higher on a standardised FP measure (d = 0.66; d = 0.72 for the benign factor and d = 0.48 for the malign factor). This result agrees with the main finding of these earlier studies, which linked IC history to presence-related experience, although the present study and these earlier studies differ in theoretical framework, instruments, and population. A post hoc comparison indicates that the ICgroup difference in FP is larger than the corresponding difference in dissociation, although the rank-based comparison was not significant. Because the present study and the earlier studies used different measures and samples, their agreement cannot be explained by the use of similar instruments or samples, and we regard this agreement as the main contribution of the present study.

The Introduction argued that an origin of ICs in bodily self-consciousness would be favoured only if all three predictions were supported. The continuity prediction (Hypothesis 3), that adults with a childhood IC history would show higher FP propensity, was clearly supported. The peripersonal prediction (Hypothesis 1), that IC locations would fall mostly within peripersonal space, received moderate support that depended on how the distance reports were coded and where the peripersonal boundary was set. The perspectival prediction (Hypothesis 2), that IC interactions would be reported mostly from a body-referenced perspective, received only weak support. The data are therefore compatible with such an origin but support it only weakly. The discussion below rests on the confirmatory findings and treats the exploratory results as directions for further research.

4.1 Peripersonal Anchoring and The Front-Back Dissociation

The evidence that ICs were localised within peripersonal space was weaker when distance entries for directions in which the companion never appeared were excluded than when all entries were included. Two-thirds of occurrence reports fell within 70 cm, a proportion modestly above one half whose significance depended on analytic choices (Section 3.2); the median of 12 cm and the 76.1% obtained when every entry was counted were produced largely by entries of 0 cm for directions the companion never occupied. Lateral reports lay mostly within reach, whereas frontal reports were evenly divided between near and far, but this post hoc contrast is not interpreted.

Because most estimates were marks on the printed scale, they support near-far rather than metric conclusions. The frequency ratings show that companions occurred mainly in the horizontal plane, also among participants who reported an occurrence (Section 3.2, which reports the spatial results), and this is consistent with the organisation of PPS around the lateral reaching zone (di Pellegrino & Làdavas, 2015; Rizzolatti et al., 1997). The animal-and monster-dominant content profile observed here contrasts with the humanoid-dominant distribution typical of Western IC samples (Bender & Vogel, 1941; Taylor, 1999) and aligns more closely with the patterns documented in non-Western samples (Davis et al., 2026); imaginary companions are also common among children outside Western settings, although their rates vary widely between countries (Wigger, 2018). Turning from content to location, a notable spatial contrast emerges when the present IC findings are compared with the established phenomenology of adult FP. In the current study, ICpositive participants localized their companions predominantly in front and to the side along the horizontal plane, with behind ratings the lowest of the four horizontal directions. On the other hand, FP is consistently reported behind or beside the body across neurological (Blanke et al., 2014), clinical (Fénelon et al., 2010; Cheyne & Girard, 2007), and non-clinical populations (Alderson-Day et al., 2023; Brederoo et al., 2024). This spatial dissociation does not by itself undermine a continuity account, and it may be informative about the mechanisms involved.

The account of this dissociation developed below should be regarded as an interpretive hypothesis rather than as evidence for a specific mechanism. The front-back dissociation rests on a between-phenomenon comparison, contrasting IC spatial estimates obtained here with FP localisation patterns documented in separate studies using different samples, measures, and methods. No within-study comparison is possible from these data. Whether frontal and posterior localisation map differentially onto hierarchical levels of predictive processing warrants direct empirical test in a design that measures both phenomena in the same participants. Frontal occurrence reports were as often beyond 70 cm as within it, so the account below concerns the direction of IC localisation rather than its distance, and it does not require frontal companions to lie within peripersonal space. With that caveat, one way to interpret this dissociation is in terms of the level of the predictive hierarchy at which the agent representation is generated. FP is thought to arise from low-level sensorimotor prediction errors: disrupted forward-model comparators at the temporoparietal junction may cause the brain's own body signals to be misattributed to an external agent (Arzy et al., 2006; Blanke et al., 2014). Such errors would be most likely to persist in posterior peripersonal space, where the absence of visual reafference prevents the correction of ambiguous proprioceptive and tactile signals (Blanke, 2012; Serino, 2019). The feeling of presence would thus inherit the spatial coordinates of maximum sensorimotor ambiguity. ICs, by contrast, might arise from high-level social-cognitive generative models sustained by mentalizing, visual imagination, and dialogic engagement (Taylor, 1999; Fernyhough et al., 2019). Because social cognition is organized around face-to-face interaction (due to the canonical configuration for shared gaze, conversation, and joint attention), the generative model might project the imagined agent into forward interactive space.

The architecture of peripersonal space itself might further contribute to this dissociation.

Front-space PPS supports action planning and social engagement, whereas back-space PPS serves primarily defensive and vigilance functions under conditions of greater perceptual uncertainty (Graziano & Cooke, 2006; de Vignemont & Iannetti, 2015). These functional properties would be expected to scaffold, respectively, a voluntarily imagined social partner and an involuntarily detected ambiguous agent. Little et al. (2021) previously compared childhood IC accounts with ghostly episode reports across multiple phenomenological dimensions, including spatial characteristics. The present data extend that comparative work by supplying distance estimates along six body-centred axes, permitting the peripersonal-extrapersonal distinction to be evaluated against an independently established boundary rather than inferred from descriptive accounts, although the coarseness of those estimates limits them to a near-far classification. Convergence across these two measurement approaches is more informative than either alone, since the methods have non-overlapping weaknesses. Direct within-study comparisons of both phenomena remain a task for future research.

Taken together, a modest near-body bias, a body-referenced majority on a perspective item whose format favoured it, and elevated FP propensity are compatible with a developmental predictive processing hypothesis. Under this hypothesis, the contrast between frontal and lateral IC localisation and posterior adult FP might reflect the development of bodily self-consciousness.

During the period of peak IC prevalence (ages 3-8), children's body representations are still maturing: PPS boundaries are not yet fully calibrated (Gabbard et al., 2007), and BSC components do not reach adult levels until approximately age 10-11 (Cowie et al., 2016; Gottwald et al., 2021).

Children's more malleable BSC and shallower PPS gradients (Cowie et al., 2016; Gabbard et al., 2007) could permit voluntary projection of agents into interactive space without requiring sensorimotor disruption. As BSC matures and multisensory body representations become more tightly constrained by visual verification, the generation of a perceived other may increasingly require an actual disruption to self-processing and the resulting presence would accordingly appear in posterior space, where the disruption is not visually resolved. This developmental plasticity may provide favorable conditions for the brain's generative models to incorporate internally generated agent representations within near-body space. Whether this proposed hierarchical account fully explains the front-back dissociation, or whether additional factors such as sensory modality dominance, cultural expectations, or individual differences in PPS boundary characteristics also play a role, are questions that warrant targeted investigation in future work.

4.2 Posterior Localisation: A Hypothesis for Future Work

The front-back dissociation described in Section 4.1 can also be approached by distinguishing a general account of continuity, on which any IC history raises adult FP propensity, from a spatially specific account, on which the elevation is concentrated among people whose companions occupied the space behind the body. The specific account has independent motivation: the space behind the body lies within reach but outside the visual field, so signals arising there cannot be checked against vision, and it is where robot-induced presence is generated (Blanke et al., 2014) and where spontaneous FP is typically located (Alderson-Day et al., 2023). The present study was not designed or powered to distinguish the accounts. The exploratory associations between behind-axis frequency and SenPQ scores were not significant (Section 3.6.3), and differences among the six directions were not tested. We therefore offer the spatially specific account only as a hypothesis; testing it requires a design measuring IC localisation and adult FP phenomenology in the same individuals, with adequate power in the posterior-localisation subgroup.

4.3 Embodied Perspective

Most participants (88.9%) reported IC interactions from a perspective that included their own bodily viewpoint. However, because of the limits of Item 38 (Section 3.3, which reports the visual perspective results, and Section 5, which discusses the limitations of the study), Hypothesis 2 is supported only weakly and within the item's response format.

A second concern is that a body-referenced report may reflect the perspective of present recall rather than that of the original past IC experience. Autobiographical memories shift toward an observer (third-person) perspective with increasing temporal distance (Nigro & Neisser, 1983; Rice & Rubin, 2009; Robinson & Swanson, 1993), which would, if anything, bias retrospective reports away from the pattern observed here. This shift is moderate rather than categorical (Piolino et al., 2006; Rice & Rubin, 2009), is attenuated for emotionally intense and self-relevant experiences (D' Argembeau et al., 2003; Libby & Eibach, 2002; Sutin & Robins, 2010; Talarico et al., 2004), and has been documented for specific episodic memories rather than for the generic memory of a repeated experience that Item 38 probes (Brewer, 1986; Conway, 2005; Neisser, 1981). Events encoded from the body's own viewpoint also tend to be recalled from it (Bergouignan et al., 2014 (Bergouignan et al., , 2022)). Because Item 38 does not separate the perspective of the original experience from that of present recall, the finding is consistent with, rather than diagnostic of, an embodied first-person organisation of the original IC experience.

4.4 Perceptual Modality and Agent-Generation Propensity

In the modality analysis, participants who experienced their IC as involving both visual and non-visual (ghost-like/sensed) qualities had the highest mean SenPQ scores, but the omnibus Kruskal-Wallis test was not significant, and with subgroup sizes of 13, 13, and 7 the analysis was severely underpowered. The pairwise difference between the sensed-only and both groups follows a non-significant omnibus test and is not interpreted. Whether multi-modal IC experience indexes a more elaborated capacity for generating internal social-agent representations requires a study designed and powered for that comparison; the "deep" IC subtype described by Lange et al. (2023), which is likewise defined by phenomenological elaborateness across sensory channels, offers a natural point of comparison.

For the continuity of agent propensity, IC-positive adults showed elevated SenPQ scores across both benign and malign subscales, suggesting that what is elevated is the underlying generative propensity for social-agent representations rather than a valence-specific quality, although the two factor-level effects were not compared statistically. The exploratory logistic regression was consistent with this: SenPQ was the sole significant predictor of IC status. Yamaguchi et al. (2023) reported that anthropomorphic tendencies, together with perceived stress, explained whether young adults currently had an imaginary companion. The present study reports that a history of childhood ICs is associated with adult FP propensity. The two findings are related in that each links IC experience to an adult individual difference, and both involve the attribution of agency to input that does not warrant it. They are not equivalent: anthropomorphism concerns the attribution of mental states to non-agents, whereas FP concerns the experience of an agent in the absence of sensory evidence. Whether these reflect a common underlying disposition is a plausible hypothesis that neither study tests, since neither measured both constructs. The conclusion from the DIS-Q comparison on its own is limited to excluding differences larger than about half a standard deviation. Its interval (d = 0.12, 95% CI [-0.22, 0.45]) does not exclude a small difference. The discriminant claim rests instead on the post hoc comparative test, in which the IC-related difference was larger for FP propensity than for dissociative tendency (difference in d = 0.55, 95% CI [0.07, 1.03]), although on a rank-based metric the difference was not significant (Section 3.5). The SenPQ and DIS-Q shared little variance on either the Pearson or the Spearman estimate (r = .14; ρ = -.04), consistent with the separation of presence phenomena from dissociative tendency reported by Alderson-Day et al. (2023).

5. Limitations and Future Directions

Several limitations point to directions for future work. First, mental boundary structure, which Drinkwater et al. (2024) identify as an important variable in the IC-anomalous experience relationship, was not measured, and measuring it would show whether the regularities reported here reflect peripersonal organisation or a broader boundary-related disposition. Second, the Turkish SenPQ adaptation (α = .911) was prepared without a documented translation protocol, and neither it nor the IC-Q, written in Turkish for this study, has yet been validated; the English version of the IC-Q (Appendix A) is a reader's translation. Formal validation would strengthen future use of both instruments.

Secondly, all IC reports were retrospective, given on average 13 to 16 years after the experience (mean age 22.8 years; companions began at 6.6 and ended at 10.1 years), so recall and reconstruction may have shaped them (Taylor, 1999; Yamaguchi et al., 2023).

Third, the IC-positive group was predominantly female, with only five men, so the findings may not generalise to men, and gender moderation of the IC-FP association could not be tested (interaction b = -5.02, 95% CI [-23.26, 13.21]). The IC-SenPQ difference nevertheless held among women alone (d = 0.55, 95% CI [0.18, 0.92]) and with gender controlled, so the main result is robust for women, although its extension to men remains untested. The female predominance is in line with the higher IC prevalence reported among girls (Ames & Learned, 1946; Bender & Vogel, 1941; Hurlock & Burstein, 1932; but see Davis et al., 2026), and samples with more men would show whether the associations hold across genders.

Fourth, the sample came from a single Turkish university, and because IC frequency and form vary across cultures (Davis et al., 2026; Hoff, 2004; Moriguchi & Todo, 2018 , 2019; Wigger, 2018 Wigger, , 2019)), replication in diverse samples is a natural next step and future research.

Fifth, recruitment materials named imaginary companions as the topic, which may have raised both the observed prevalence (24.3%; Moriguchi & Todo, 2018) and the IC-SenPQ association, so the effect sizes are best treated as upper bounds until topic-blind replication. Future administrations should also add automated bot screening, such as duplicate-response detection and completion-time checks.

Sixth, each participant gave a single, uncalibrated retrospective distance estimate per axis, and 72% of occurrence reports coincided with a mark on the printed scale (1, 20, 150, 300 or 500 cm), so the data support near-far rather than metric conclusions. The Hypothesis 1 result also depended on the coding of 1 cm entries and on the analytic choices in Table D.1, partly because the distance items offered no not-applicable option (Section 2.4, which describes the analyses).

Adding such an option and an unmarked response scale would make future estimates more precise.

Seventh, visual perspective was measured with a single item, IC-Q Item 38, which does not separate the perspective of the original experience from that of present recall, so the perspectival finding is consistent with, rather than diagnostic of, an embodied first-person organisation. The inverted card headings mean that the first-person proportion is reported only descriptively, although they could not have raised the body-referenced proportion. The item offered no fixed third-person option, and three of its four fixed options were body-referenced, so the body-referenced proportion may overstate body-referenced recall. The result also depends on coding option (a) as body-referenced, and the four third-person classifications rest on a single rater.

The instrument is reproduced, with its card headings as printed, in Appendix B (see also

Table 2), and a revised item that separates encoding from retrieval and offers a fixed third-person option would permit a more rigorous test of Hypothesis 2. Future studies could also measure anthropomorphic attribution, which Yamaguchi et al. (2023) and Drinkwater et al. (2024) identify as a substantive predictor, to test whether a general disposition to attribute agency mediates the IC associations. Recording whether a companion inhabited a separate imagined world (a paracosm) would likewise distinguish companions anchored to the participant's bodily frame from companions that were not.

Participants excluded for psychiatric or neurological diagnosis showed somewhat higher dissociation scores than the retained sample (p = .062), so the DIS-Q null applies to non-clinical samples. The DIS-Q interval excludes only differences larger than about half a standard deviation, and the discriminant claim therefore rests on the comparative test (Section 3.5, which reports this test).

Finally, the exploratory findings are hypothesis-generating. The IC-positive subsample (n = 45) and the modality subgroups (ns = 13, 13, 7) afford limited power, and no directional or modality test was significant before or after correction for multiple comparisons. Prospective designs in childhood, experimental PPS paradigms with children and longitudinal follow-up could test these hypotheses directly, together with a multi-item measure of IC modality and a measure of perceived IC autonomy, which varies substantially across companions (Davies, 2023; Taylor et al., 2007; Taylor, Hodges, & Kohányi, 2003). Such measures would show whether companions experienced as extensions of the child's own agency are represented in peripersonal space and independent agents further away, and whether IC modality predicts specific subtypes of adult anomalous experience.

6. Conclusion

Children commonly report seeing and hearing their imaginary companions, which indicates that companions are experienced as sensorily present rather than merely conceived (Taylor & Aguiar, 2024). The present findings add tentative evidence on where this presence was located. Distance estimates fell somewhat more often within than beyond reach, although this margin depended, and most participants recalled their companion from a perspective that included their own viewpoint. A post hoc comparison also indicated that IC history was more strongly associated with FP propensity than with dissociative tendency, although the rank-based difference was not significant.

The present study and earlier studies of anomalous experience (Drinkwater et al., 2024; Lange et al., 2023; Laythe et al., 2021; Little et al., 2021) both suggest that a childhood IC history is associated with adult presence-related experience and that this association reflects a stable individual difference rather than pathology. Because the present study and these earlier studies differ in theoretical vocabulary, measurement and population, their convergence strengthens this conclusion.

The evidence that the association reflects the mechanisms proposed by a BSC account remains partial, and future experimental designs that measure both phenomena in the same individuals could test these mechanisms directly. the participant [Smaller / Same / Larger]; (32) Child-like or adult-like? Note. Occurrence was classified from the frequency rating that preceded each distance item (1 = never; 2-7 = occurrence). Of the 255 distance entries, 141 were given for directions rated never: 90 of the 92 entries of 0 cm, 15 of the 29 entries of 1 cm, and 36 other values (17 of them 500 cm). Two entries of 0 cm and 14 of 1 cm were given for occurring directions and are retained under the rule; three participants rated every direction as never. Clustered estimates are from generalised estimating equations (binomial family, exchangeable working correlation, clustered by participant) testing the proportion of reports within the boundary against .50. Participant-level tests use each participant's median distance: an exact sign test against 50% and a Wilcoxon signed-rank test against 70 cm, whose symmetry assumption is violated under every coding (skewness of participant medians 3.1 with all entries, 2.4 under the occurrence rule). Most entries coincide with marks on the distance scale printed on the illustrative cards (1, 20, 150, 300, and 500 cm). Because no occurrence report lies between 50 and 80 cm, or between 30 and 40 cm, or between 100 and 120 cm, boundaries within each of those ranges give identical results. Panel B, final columns: percentage of entries within the boundary under the two alternative codings. The coding that also excludes 1-cm entries is reported as an additional test here, because 11 of the 14 entries of 1 cm for occurring directions came from participants who, for the directions they rated as never, either entered only 0 or 500 cm (9 entries) or left the distance blank (2 entries), so that for them 1 cm appears to denote a genuine near placement. With all entries counted as locations, the pooled median distance was 12 cm; this coding is shown for comparison only, because it counts entries for directions in which the companion never appeared as near-body locations.

Data Availability Statement.

The de-identified participant-level dataset, the pooled directional distance file, the directional frequency-rating file, the Python analysis code with a single script that reruns every analysis, an annotated codebook, the illustrative cards used with the spatial and perspective items (IC-Q Item 38 both as administered and with corrected card headings), and a reproducibility report that lists each statistic computed from the deposited data with the script and output that produce it are deposited in the OSF project at https://osf.io/qwynu (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/QWYNU) and mirrored on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23213806). A preprint of this work is available at https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/7fsem_v2 (https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/7fsem_v2); an updated version will be posted on acceptance. Free-text responses require further de-identification before deposition and will be withheld or redacted accordingly. The Turkish-adapted SenPQ and DIS-Q are reproduced from copyrighted instruments and can be shared only to the extent the rights holders permit; the IC-Q, which was developed for this study, is reproduced in full in Appendices A and B. Values that depend on data not in the deposit (the comparison with excluded participants in Section 2.1 and counts coded from withheld free text) are identified as such in the reproducibility report.

The authors have no conflicts of interest to disclose.

Appendix A IC Questionnaire (IC-Q)

A 39-item Turkish-language questionnaire administered to IC-positive participants, with content adapted from Taylor (1999) and Hoff (2004) and supplemented with items assessing spatial localization and visual perspective developed for the present study. The IC-Q was written and administered in Turkish; the English version given here is a reader's translation and has not been validated for administration. Six items contain conditional follow-up sub-items (3a/b, 6a, 16a, 30a, 33a, 34a).

modelled the structural relationships underlying the ICanomalous experience association and reported a best-fitting path model running from thin mental boundaries, through creative experiences, to IC report, and thence to entity-encounter experiences. Two features of that model matter here. First, the Drinkwater et al. (2024) model locates IC experience as a mediator rather than an endpoint. Second, it identifies boundary structure as a distal individual-difference variable that could in principle account for regularities in IC phenomenology without appeal to the spatial mechanisms proposed here.

and demographic information, all participants completed the DIS-Q and SenPQ. Participants who endorsed a history of childhood imaginary companions then completed the IC-Q, including the spatial localization and visual perspective sections. No automated bot-screening controls were implemented in the survey instrument: the form did not use CAPTCHA, attention-check items, completion-time thresholds, or duplicate-response detection. Participants were recruited through course-credit announcements circulated on a closed institutional channel within a single university department, rather than through an open web link or a commercial panel; this materially reduces, without eliminating, exposure to automated responding. The recruitment materials named imaginary companions as the topic of the study (see Limitations). The instrument additionally contained a large number of open-ended items whose free-text responses were inspected for coherence during coding. This absence of formal screening is recorded as a limitation.

Did you have a pet at home during the IC period? [Yes/No];

If yes, what kind of pet?

Section 2: IC Identity and Temporal Characteristics (Items 7-11)

Number of ICs [Open]; (8) Name(s) of the IC, or how the participant addressed the IC [Open];

Ongoing contact with the IC at the time of the study? [Yes/No];

Age at IC onset [Years];

Age at IC disappearance [Years].

Section 3: Interaction and Sensory Modality (Items 12-16a) (12) Was the IC visible to others? [Yes/No]; (13) Did the IC also exist as a real toy or object? [Yes/No];

Tactile interaction with the IC? [Yes/No]; (15) Did the IC have an odor? [Yes/No]; (16) Was the IC visually perceived or sensed in the environment without visual content? [Sensed like a ghost / Visible / Both / Neither];

Section 4: Spatial Localization (Items 17-29) (17) Direction(s) in which the IC was felt relative to the body [multi-select: front / behind / below / above / right / left]. Items 18-29 then collect, for each of these six directions in sequence (front, behind, below, above, right, left), one frequency rating on a 7-point scale (1 = never,7 = very often), and one distance estimate in centimeters, yielding six frequency-distance pairs. Frequency items: 18 (front), 20 (behind), 22 (below), 24 (above), 26 (right), 28 (left). Distance items: 19, 21, 23, 25, 27, 29. Section 5: Appearance and Behavior (Items 30-35) (30) Form of the IC [Animal / Human / Toy / Monster / Other]; (30a) If "Other" was selected at Item 30, describe how the IC's form changed over time [Open];

Size relative to Hayali arkadaşınızı gördüğünüz süre boyunca evde evcil hayvanınız var mıydı? [Evet / Hayır];

Bir önceki soruya evet cevabını verdiyseniz lütfen hangi hayvan türü olduğunu belirtiniz. [Açık uçlu].

Bölüm 2: Hayali Arkadaşın Kimliği ve Zamansal Özellikleri (Maddeler 7-11)

Kaç tane hayali arkadaşınız vardı? [Açık uçlu]; (8) Hayali arkadaş(lar)ınıza nasıl hitap ediyordunuz? İsmi varsa lütfen yazınız. [Açık uçlu];

Hayali arkadaş(lar)ınızla hâlâ arada iletişim kuruyor musunuz? [Evet / Hayır];

Hayali arkadaş(lar)ınızla tanıştığınızda kaç yaşındaydınız? [Yıl];

Eğer artık hayali arkadaşınızla oynamıyorsanız, ortadan kaybolduklarında kaç yaşındaydınız? [Yıl].

Bölüm 3: Etkileşim ve Duyusal Modalite (Maddeler 12-16a)

Hayali arkadaş(lar)ınız başkalarına da görünüyor muydu? [Evet / Hayır]; (13) Hayali arkadaşınız gerçek hayatta bir oyuncak veya obje olarak da var mıydı? [Evet / Hayır];

Hayali arkadaşınız size dokunabiliyor muydu ya da siz ona dokunduğunuzu hissediyor muydunuz? [Evet / Hayır]; (15) Hayali arkadaşınızın kokusu var mıydı? [Evet / Hayır];

Hayali arkadaşınız size görünüyor muydu yoksa bir hayalet gibi onun varlığını bulunduğunuz ortamın içinde hissedebiliyor muydunuz? [Hissedebiliyordum / Görebiliyordum / Her ikisi de / Hiçbiri];

Bir önceki soruya HİÇBİRİ cevabını verdiyseniz lütfen bu duyguyu tanımlayınız. [Açık uçlu].

Hayali arkadaşınızı kendi bedeninize göre nerede hissediyordunuz? [Çoktan seçmeli, uygun olanların tümü: Önümde / Arkamda / Aşağımda / Yukarımda / Sağımda / Solumda].

Maddeler 18-29 daha sonra bu altı yön için sırayla (önde, arkada, aşağıda, yukarıda, sağda, solda) birer sıklık derecelendirmesi ve birer mesafe tahmini toplamaktadır. Sıklık maddeleri: "Hayali arkadaşınızı kendi bedeninize göre ne sıklıkla [yön] hissediyordunuz? (1 = hiç hissetmiyordum,7 = çok sık hissediyordum)" Madde 18 (önümde), 20 (arkamda), 22 (aşağımda), 24 (yukarımda), 26 (sağımda), 28 (solumda). Mesafe maddeleri: "Hayali arkadaşınızı kendi bedeninize göre ne kadar mesafede [yön] hissediyordunuz? (Santimetre cinsinden belirtiniz)" -Madde 19, 21, 23, 25, 27, 29. Bölüm 5: Görünüm ve Davranış (Maddeler 30-35)

Hayali arkadaşınızın boyutu ne kadardı? [Benden küçük / Benim kadar / Benden büyük];

Hayali arkadaşınız fiziksel hareketlerinizi taklit ediyor muydu (siz koşunca koşması vb.)? [Evet / Hayır];

Bir önceki soruya evet cevabını verdiyseniz lütfen örnek veriniz. [Açık uçlu];

Hayali arkadaşınız fiziksel pozisyonunuzu/postürünüzü taklit ediyor muydu (siz kalkınca kalkması vb.)? [Evet / Hayır];

Bir önceki soruya evet cevabını verdiyseniz lütfen örnek veriniz. [Açık uçlu];

Hayali arkadaşım… [erkekti / kadındı / Diğer].

Bölüm 6: İletişim ve Görsel Bakış Açısı (Maddeler 36-38)

Kendi aranızda konuşuyor muydunuz? [Evet / Hayır]; (37) Gizli bir diliniz var mıydı? [Evet / Hayır];

"Hayali arkadaşım yanımdayken…" dört seçenek ve bir açık uçlu alan ile sunulmuştur: (a) "Olayları onun bakış açısından da algılayabiliyordum."; (b) "Olayları sadece kendi bakış açımdan algılayabiliyordum."; (c) "Hatırlamıyorum"; (d) "Her ikisi de"; (e) "Diğer" [Açık uçlu].

Madde, her iki bakış açısı seçeneğini gösteren birer görsel kart ile birlikte sunulmuştur
